notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on 1 John 4. A few gaps first: my searches turned up no pages from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org or the Lutheran sites. I found nothing describing a hyper-grace or word-of-faith reading of any verse. The only Catholic-side voice is Augustine (on ccel.org), so the notes say less about those views than you asked for.

**v. 1**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says we should never assume that every spiritual experience or show of power comes from God. Every Christian has to test them, and church leaders most of all, using Scripture as the standard. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/
- The Pulpit Commentary says "the spirits" are principles and tendencies in religion, and being earnest or fervent doesn't prove they're true. Testing them is the duty of the individual Christian as well as of the Church in its official capacity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_john/4.htm
- Precept Austin quotes Hiebert: speaking spirits were well known in the pagan world of John's day. It also notes that the Greek tense for "gone out" means these prophets left at a point in time and are still active. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/59510/

**v. 2**
- Guzik: true teaching presents a true Jesus. In John's day, the issue was about if Jesus had *truly* come in a *real* body of flesh and blood. He quotes Boice, who links this to Docetism. Guzik adds that this was the pressing test in John's day, not the only test of false doctrine. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/
- Precept Austin also describes Docetism as the teaching that Jesus only "appeared" to have a human body, and says John directly refuted this false teaching in 1Jn 4:2-3. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-4-commentary

**v. 3**
- Pulpit (scholarly/textual note): the best reading is simply "does not confess Jesus." The longer wording is a later addition copied from the verse before. An ancient variant, known to Irenaeus and Tertullian, reads "dissolves Jesus." It was aimed at people who split the man Jesus from the divine Christ, but the Greek manuscripts all reject it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_john/4.htm
- Guzik: the antichrist spirit opposes the true Jesus and offers a substitute. It is already at work wherever a false Jesus is preached, even though it will peak in a final end-times ruler. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/

**v. 4**
- Guzik: the "greater one" is the indwelling Spirit or Jesus. Victory is always possible if we rely on Him rather than on ourselves, so Christians have no reason for fear. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/
- Pulpit reads "have overcome them" literally. The believers refused to listen, and the false teachers left the church. Pulpit says John allows no neutral ground between truth and error. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_john/4.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: just because the world listens to a message doesn't make it God's message. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/
- Pulpit: false teachers draw their ideas from the world, which is why the world listens. It compares John 15:19. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_john/4.htm

**v. 6 (a point Protestants and Catholics dispute)**
- Pulpit: "we" here seems to mean the apostles, since if it meant all believers, nobody would be left to do the hearing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_john/4.htm
- Guzik agrees that "we" means the apostles and their teaching as recorded in the Bible. He rejects the Roman Catholic Church's claim to be the "us." This is a Protestant description of the Catholic view; I found no Catholic source. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/

**v. 7**
- Guzik: the Greek begins "beloved, let us love." We love because we are already loved, not to earn God's love. New birth gives a love we didn't have before. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/
- Pulpit: the call to love is secondary to the main truth, "God is love." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_john/4.htm

**v. 8 (Arminian vs. Calvinist)**
- Pulpit: don't water "God is love" down to "God is loving." Love is God's very nature, not just one of His qualities. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_john/4.htm
- Guzik: love colours all of God's nature but doesn't cancel His holiness or justice. He warns against turning the phrase around into "love is God." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/
- Adam Clarke (Methodist), as quoted by Guzik, uses this verse against any decree of unconditional reprobation, saying God has made no human being for perdition. I didn't find a Reformed answer to this on these pages. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: "among us" means "in our case." The verse could summarise John's Gospel, and the key words are "only begotten" and "live." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_john/4.htm
- Guzik: "only begotten" means Jesus shares the Father's nature, unlike our adopted sonship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/

**v. 10**
- Guzik: the Father sent the Son not on a mission of compassion but to die for our sins, as the propitiation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/
- Precept Austin quotes James Denney: the verse is a paradox, because God is at once loving and wrathful, and His love provides the propitiation which averts His wrath from us. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_john_410_commentary

**v. 11**
- Precept Austin quotes the NET Bible note: God's sacrifice ought to motivate us as believers to love one another in a similar sacrificial fashion. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_john_411_commentary
- Pulpit: the "if" carries no doubt. You'd expect John to say "love God," but he skips that as obvious. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_john/4.htm

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: "His love" here means our love for God, which matures as we love our brothers and sisters. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_john/4.htm
- Guzik: the greatest evidence of God's presence is love, not power, popularity or strong feelings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/
- Precept Austin quotes Barclay: we can't see God, only His effects, the way we see what the wind does. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_john_412_commentary

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: John says "of His Spirit" because only Christ has the Spirit in full. Pulpit also sees four things that go together in the chapter: confessing the Incarnation, having the Spirit, loving others, and God living in us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_john/4.htm
- Precept Austin quotes Stott: the same Spirit leads us to confess the Incarnation and enables us to love. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_john_413_commentary

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: "we" means the apostles who saw Christ with their own eyes. "The world" means mainly unregenerate people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_john/4.htm
- Precept Austin wonders whether the phrase "Savior of the world" recalls the Samaritans in John 4. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-4-commentary

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: the sense is someone who has once for all taken their stand as a confessor. Verse 14 is the apostles' witness, verse 15 is those who accept it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_john/4.htm
- Guzik: love isn't enough without the true confession. We need both truth and love. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/

**v. 16**
- Pulpit: "know and believe" describes an ongoing state. Love is not only the mark of the Church but its creed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_john/4.htm
- Gill notes the Syriac version leaves out "and God in him." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_john/4-16.htm
- Augustine (a Church Father read by Catholics and Orthodox) reads the verse as "Love is God" and says: let God be your house, and be a house for God. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf107.iv.xii.html

**v. 17 (the most debated verse)**
- Calvin (Reformed): the boldness comes from being sure of God's fatherly love. Being renewed in God's image confirms that we are His children, but only as a secondary support. He says Catholics wrongly use this verse to rest assurance on works, and that confidence must rest on grace alone. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom45/calcom45.v.v.v.html
- Augustine: "as He is" means a likeness, not equality. It means loving our enemies as God does, so that we come to long for judgment day instead of dreading it. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf107.iv.xii.html
- Guzik reads it as our standing now: Jesus is glorified, justified, forever righteous and bold, and we share that standing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/
- Gill holds several senses together: believers are in Christ by representation, righteous in Him, and called to be like Him. Barnes takes it as sharing Christ's character. Clarke (Methodist) says it means being saved from sin and made holy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-john/4-17.html
- Precept Austin quotes Piper: confidence comes when God's love reaches its goal in action rather than just talk. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_john_417_commentary

**v. 18 (a real Protestant split)**
- Traditional reading: Gill keeps the healthy "filial" fear of God, a child's reverence, and says what love removes is fear of men, of death and of judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_john/4-18.htm Spurgeon also says the word "fear" is used in different senses, so Proverbs and John don't contradict each other. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/the-right-kind-of-fear/
- Calvin openly rejects using this verse for the "servile vs. filial fear" distinction. He says the love here is God's love for us, known by faith, which calms the conscience. His English editor disagrees and says most commentators take it as our own love. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom45/calcom45.v.v.v.html
- Methodist and Holiness: Clarke sets out stages, from penitents who have fear without love, to new converts with mixed fear, to adult Christians have love without this fear, and points readers to Wesley's note on this verse. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/1-john/4-18.html Godbey (Holiness) goes further: the fear is the depravity, which is destroyed in sanctification. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/msg/1-john/4-19.html
- Barnes doubts that love will fully cast out fear in anyone before heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_john/4-18.htm
- Augustine: fear comes first and makes room for love, like a needle drawing a thread through. As love grows, fear shrinks. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf107.iv.xii.html

**v. 19**
- Precept Austin quotes Steven Cole: God is the source of all love, so if you struggle to love someone, think about the love God showed you at the cross. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_john_419_commentary

**v. 20**
- Guzik: if we claim to love God but don't love His people, we are lying. Visible love for His people is the proof of love for the invisible God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-4/

**v. 21**
- I didn't find anything verse-specific beyond Guzik's general comment on loving one another. Augustine's homily covers this verse too, but the page I read cut off before it. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf107.iv.xii.html
